conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Patel, a mental-health clinician who specializes in the emotional changes that can happen after a baby arrives. I’d like to spend a few minutes with you on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually just called the EPDS. It’s a brief, well-studied set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling physically and emotionally over the past seven days.  

Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in immediate danger, so please answer as openly as you feel comfortable. There are no right or wrong answers—only what’s true for you. When we’re finished, we’ll talk about what your responses might mean and any next steps that could be helpful.  

Ready? Let’s start with the first question:  

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft sigh, eyes down for a second]

Lately… it’s been pretty hard. I’ll catch myself half-smiling at something on my phone, but it fades fast—like I can’t really feel it. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find anything funny.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

No… not really. I put “no, not so much lately.” I can’t remember the last time I actually laughed.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice quiet]

Not really. Even the little things I used to like—coffee out, a show I followed—feel kind of… flat. I keep thinking, “What’s the point? I’ll just be too tired or worried anyway.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes flick to the floor, voice tight]

Yeah… a lot. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I missed something—wrong swaddle, didn’t burp her long enough, ate something funny. My husband says I’m doing fine, but I keep replaying every little hiccup and telling myself I should’ve known better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[nods slowly, twisting a tissue in my hands]

Pretty much every day. Sometimes it’s just this knot in my chest that she’s not breathing, or that I’ll drop her, or that the formula isn’t the right temperature—even when everything looks fine. I’ll check the monitor three, four times a night, convinced something’s wrong even though I know it’s not rational.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[breath catches]

Yes… a few times. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get enough air. Nothing triggers it—once I was just folding her tiny socks—and suddenly I’m sure something awful is about to happen. It passes after a minute, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]

Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, she won’t nap, I haven’t showered—everything feels too heavy, like I’m one cry-session away from completely falling apart. I keep telling myself moms handle this, but I can’t seem to stay afloat.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[eyes well up a little]

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop. I keep replaying every little thing I might’ve done wrong, or I’m sure I hear her crying when the monitor’s quiet. I finally drift off, then jolt awake for her feeding and can’t get back to sleep even after she’s settled.
I have felt sad or miserable

[quiet, shaky voice]

Yes… most of the week. It’s like this gray cloud that just sits there. I’ll be feeding her and tears start rolling without any real reason. I miss feeling like “me,” but I’m also guilty for being sad when I’ve got this healthy baby.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods, dabbing at my eyes with the crumpled tissue]

Yeah… it’s been most days. Sometimes it’s just quiet tears while I rock her at 3 a.m.; other times I have to hand her to my husband and go sob in the bathroom because I feel like I’m failing her and I can’t explain why.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—no, never. I feel low, but I’d never want to leave her. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: Patient self-report, 10-item EPDS-style interview (responses recorded verbatim).

Symptoms / Behaviors endorsed  
- Marked anhedonia: absent laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment  
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” daily tearfulness  
- Excessive self-blame and guilt re infant care  
- Chronic, intrusive anxiety (health/safety of infant), physical tension  
- Discrete panic episodes (sudden racing heart, breathlessness)  
- Overwhelm / feeling “drowning in small stuff,” coping perceived as inadequate  
- Sleep initiation/maintenance impaired by ruminations and hypervigilance  
- Subjective sense of identity loss (“miss feeling like ‘me’”)  

Frequency / Duration  
- Present “most days” for ≥2 weeks (patient unable to specify onset)  
- Crying spells: daily, including nocturnal  
- Panic attacks: “a few times,” sudden onset, self-limited  

Safety  
- Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation (Q10: “No—no, never”)  
- No homicidal ideation reported  

Risk factors noted  
- Primiparous status, infant ≤3 months implied  
- Perfectionistic self-expectations, limited perceived support  
- Sleep deprivation secondary to mood rather than infant demands alone  

Screening Impression  
High likelihood of clinically significant postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; symptoms exceed “baby blues” threshold, cause marked distress and functional impairment. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment and safety plan today.
